title: Why Do Kids Have So Many Days Off?
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman observes that school calendars are getting longer without giving students more school. Counting 26 discretionary days off in his own Fairfax County district beyond federal holidays, he summarizes his analysis for The 74 of calendars in DC-area districts and the ten largest districts nationally. Compared with pre-pandemic schedules, many districts have stretched the same roughly 180 days across a longer span with more long weekends. Aldeman notes the thin research base, pointing to four-day week studies where learning losses seem driven by reduced instructional time, and to districts that lengthened calendars without adding student time. His sharper point is from the parent's perspective: summer is a predictable childcare challenge with an industry built around it, while scattered Mondays, Fridays, and teacher workdays are harder for working parents to manage. He closes by flagging the mixed message this sends while schools try to rebuild norms of regular attendance.
points: Fairfax County's calendar includes 26 discretionary days off in addition to seven federal holidays, not counting snow days or early dismissals.
Many districts have spread roughly 180 days over a longer calendar with more long weekends rather than adding instructional time.
Four-day week research suggests learning losses largely stem from reduced instructional time.
Scattered days off are harder for working parents than summer, which is at least predictable and served by camps and programs.
Frequent interruptions undercut schools' efforts to re-establish norms of regular attendance.
quotes: Over the course of the year, I count 26 “discretionary” days off, not including seven federal holidays such as Labor Day and Columbus Day. And that doesn’t include unplanned snow days or early dismissals.
Does this matter? It does to the families I know at my kids’ bus stops! They’re more likely to complain about random days off or early dismissals than the latest test scores.
All those interruptions create difficult choices for parents when their kids are home but they have to work.

Students tend to learn somewhat less under four-day schedules, but much of that effect appears to come from reductions in total instructional time. It is notable, though, that many districts extended their calendar but chose not to add any extra time for students.
Summer is a long childcare challenge, but at least it is predictable, and an entire range of camps and programs exists to accommodate it.

A growing collection of random Mondays and Friday offs, teacher workdays and four-day weekends can be harder to manage, especially for parents who can’t work from home or take 20-plus days off during the school year.
